title: No-Code App Development
subtitle: Plan, build, test and hand over a working business app on Google AppSheet, and price it as paid client work.
description: You learn to judge when a business needs an app, design its data model, and build a complete stock and sales app on Google AppSheet with calculations, validation rules and an automatic alert. You then test, secure and document it, and learn to run discovery, price projects and plan your first 90 days of no-code client work.
outcomes: Decide whether a business problem needs a spreadsheet, a form, a no-code app or custom code
Design a data model with tables, keys, references and correct column types
Build an AppSheet app with views, expressions, Valid If rules, actions and a bot
Test an app with edge cases, control access, configure offline use and write a handover pack
Run client discovery, write a one-page specification and price a build with milestones
Present demo apps and case studies and follow a 90-day plan toward paid work
audience: Women with solid spreadsheet and smartphone skills who want to build internal business apps for their own work, employers or paying clients.
tools: A Google account with Google Sheets
A laptop or desktop for building (the AppSheet editor works best on a larger screen)
An Android phone or iPhone with the AppSheet app for testing
Free AppSheet prototyping (up to 10 test users)
Paper and pen for data models and process maps

modules.title: No-Code Foundations: Problems, Data and Platforms
modules.overview: Before you open any builder, you need to judge whether an app is the right answer, and you need to think in tables, keys and links the way every serious app does. This module gives you that judgement, the data modelling skill underneath every no-code platform, and a clear view of what the platforms cost and where the paid work is.

lessons.title: Spreadsheet, form, no-code app or custom code: choosing the right tool
objectives: Explain what a no-code app builder does and how it differs from low-code and custom code
Use five questions to decide whether a problem needs an app at all
Match a business need to a type of no-code platform
Name the honest limits of no-code tools before you promise a client anything

blocks.text: A **no-code app builder** lets you create a working app by choosing screens, fields and rules in a visual editor instead of writing programming code. Underneath, the app still has the same three parts every app has: **data** (the information it stores), **interface** (the screens people tap and type on) and **logic** (the rules about what happens and when). The builder writes the code for you. Your job is to design those three parts well.

A **low-code** platform works the same way but also lets a developer add custom code when the visual tools run out. **Custom code** means a programmer builds everything from scratch. Custom code can do almost anything, but it costs more, takes longer and needs a developer to maintain it. No-code is fastest and cheapest, but you live inside what the platform allows.

blocks.name: building-blocks
blocks.alt: A person assembling large building blocks
blocks.caption: No-code means building from ready-made blocks: tables, screens and rules you configure rather than code.

blocks.text: Not every problem needs an app

Advanced builders are valuable because they know when **not** to build. Many problems are solved by a well-designed spreadsheet or a simple form. An app earns its place when several people must enter and see the same data, often on phones, with rules that stop mistakes. Ask these five questions before you build anything.

items: **How many people touch the data?** One person keeping records alone can usually stay with a spreadsheet.
**Where is the work done?** If staff work in a shop, on a farm or on the road, a phone app beats a laptop spreadsheet.
**Do records link to each other?** Customers with many orders, products with many sales: linked records are where apps shine.
**Are mistakes costly?** If a wrong price or a double booking loses money, you need rules that block bad entries.
**Does the outside public need to use it?** Public, customer-facing apps raise cost and data protection duties, so plan them carefully.

blocks.title: Choosing the right tool
items: One person, simple list: spreadsheet
Collect answers only: form
Team, linked records: no-code app
Unusual logic, huge scale: custom code
blocks.caption: Move to the next tool only when the simpler one genuinely cannot do the job.

blocks.text: The main families of no-code platforms

head: Family
Examples
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Internal tools for staff: stock, orders, field visits, bookings
Paid plans are usually charged per user; check limits on rows and users
Softr on Airtable or other sources
Depends on a second tool for the data, so two subscriptions
Customer-facing web apps with sign-up and payments
Steeper learning curve, closer to real programming logic
No proper editing, linking or role control after submission

blocks.text: This course builds on **Google AppSheet**, because it reads straight from Google Sheets, runs on Android and iPhone, works offline, and lets you prototype free with up to 10 test users. The thinking you learn (data model, views, rules, testing, handover) transfers to Glide, Softr or Bubble.

blocks.title: Worked example: should Nneka's tailoring workshop get an app?
blocks.context: For example, Nneka runs a tailoring workshop in Aba with three apprentices. Customers send styles and measurements on WhatsApp. Orders are written in a notebook, and about 60 orders a month pass through the shop. Twice last month a dress was promised for the wrong date.
steps: People: Nneka and three apprentices all need to see orders, so four users. A private spreadsheet is not enough.
Place: the work happens at cutting tables, not at a desk, so phones matter.
Links: one customer has many orders, and each order has measurements and a due date. These are linked records.
Cost of mistakes: a missed delivery date loses a customer, so the app should show orders due in the next 3 days on its first screen.
Public use: customers do not need to log in. They keep using WhatsApp, which keeps the build internal and simpler.
blocks.result: An internal no-code app on AppSheet fits: four staff users, linked Customers and Orders tables, and a 'Due soon' view. A public customer app would be unnecessary cost.

blocks.text: Honest limits you must know

items: **Platform lock-in:** your app's screens and rules live on the vendor's platform. If prices rise or the product changes, moving is a rebuild, although your data in Google Sheets stays yours.
**Per-user costs:** many internal tool platforms charge per user per month, so an app for 40 staff can cost far more each year than the build fee.
**Performance:** spreadsheet-backed apps slow down as tables grow very large or formulas get heavy. Keep heavy calculations out of every row where you can.
**Complex logic:** unusual calculations, real-time features or deep integrations may need low-code or a developer.

blocks.title: Say it before the client asks
blocks.text: Professionals write the limits into the proposal: who owns the data, what the monthly platform fee is, and what would trigger a move to custom code. Clients trust a builder who names the ceiling early.

takeaways: Every app is data, interface and logic; no-code only removes the typing of code
Use the simplest tool that works: spreadsheet, then form, then no-code app, then custom code
No-code apps shine for teams working on phones with linked records and costly mistakes
State lock-in, per-user cost and performance limits before you build

activity.title: Run the five-question test
steps: Pick two real problems from a business you know (your own, a relative's or a church or cooperative).
Answer the five questions for each problem in writing.
Decide for each: spreadsheet, form, no-code app or custom code, and give one reason.
For any problem that needs an app, write the first screen a user should see and why.
activity.evidence: A one-page note with both problems, your five answers each, and your tool decision

lessons.title: Data modelling for no-code apps: tables, keys and references
objectives: Split a business's information into separate tables, one per kind of thing
Choose a unique key for every table and explain why names make poor keys
Link tables with references for one-to-many relationships
Choose the right column types so the app can validate entries

blocks.text: The **data model** is the plan of what your app stores and how the pieces connect. It is the single biggest difference between an app that grows smoothly and one that becomes a mess after three months. Good no-code builders spend more time here than on screens, because screens are easy to change and data structure is not.

blocks.name: database-tables
blocks.alt: Linked database tables on a screen
blocks.caption: A clean data model is a set of small tables, each about one kind of thing, linked by keys.

blocks.text: Rule 1: one table per kind of thing

A **table** holds one kind of thing: customers, orders, products, staff. Each **row** is one of those things and each **column** is one fact about it. In Google Sheets, each table is one tab with a single header row on top. Avoid the common beginner pattern of putting everything into one wide sheet with columns like Item1, Item2, Item3. That design breaks the day a customer brings four items.
Rule 2: every row needs a key

A **key** is a column whose value is different for every row, so the app can find exactly one record. Names make poor keys: two customers can both be called Blessing, and people change phone numbers. In AppSheet the usual practice is an ID column whose initial value is the function **UNIQUEID()**, which creates a random ID when the row is added. The user never needs to see it.
Rule 3: link tables with references

A **reference** is a column that stores the key of a row in another table. In AppSheet the column type is **Ref**. When the Orders table has a Customer column of type Ref pointing to Customers, each order belongs to one customer, and one customer can have many orders. This is a **one-to-many relationship**, the most common pattern in business apps. AppSheet then adds a related list on the customer screen so staff can see all her orders in one tap.

blocks.title: Laundry app data model
items: Customers (one)
Orders (many per customer)
Order Items (many per order)
Price List (one price per item)
blocks.caption: Each arrow is a Ref column pointing back to the key of the table before it.

blocks.title: Worked example: modelling a laundry service
blocks.context: For example, Bisi runs a laundry and dry-cleaning service in Lekki. Today she writes each pickup in a book: customer name, phone, a list of clothes and a total. She wants an app her two riders and one ironing staff can use.
steps: Tables: Customers (ID, Name, Phone, Address), Price List (ItemID, Item, Price), Orders (OrderID, Customer as Ref, Pickup Date, Status), Order Items (LineID, Order as Ref, Item as Ref, Qty).
Prices (illustrative): shirt ₦800, trousers ₦1,000, duvet ₦5,000.
An order has 4 shirts, 2 trousers and 1 duvet, entered as three Order Items rows.
Each line total is Qty times the item price: 4 × 800 = 3,200; 2 × 1,000 = 2,000; 1 × 5,000 = 5,000.
The order total adds the line totals: 3,200 + 2,000 + 5,000 = 10,200.
blocks.result: The order total is ₦10,200, worked out by the app from linked rows. Adding a fourth kind of item needs a new row, not a new column, so the model never breaks.

blocks.text: Rule 4: pick the right column type
Column types tell the app what kind of value is allowed, which gives you free checking and better phone keyboards. AppSheet offers many types; these are the ones you will use most.

head: Column type
Use it for
What it gives you
rows: Number keyboard; Price shows currency formatting
Date picker, so no '31st of February'
Status such as Received, Washing, Ready, Delivered
A fixed dropdown list, so spellings stay consistent
Tap to call or email from the app
Photo of a stained item, delivery location
Dropdown of real records and related lists

blocks.text: Stored columns and calculated columns

Store only facts that people enter. Values that can be worked out, such as a line total or an order total, should be calculated. In AppSheet you can add a **virtual column** with an **App formula**, for example a line total of [Qty] * [Item].[Price], where [Item].[Price] follows the reference to read the price. This is called **dereferencing**. Calculated values never disagree with the data they come from.

blocks.title: Price changes and old orders
blocks.text: If a line total always reads today's price from the Price List, raising the shirt price will silently change last month's orders. For money, copy the price into the Order Items row when the line is created (an initial value), so history stays true.
Sketch the model on paper first: boxes for tables, lines for references, and the key underlined in each box. If you cannot draw it, you are not ready to build it.

takeaways: One table per kind of thing; one header row per tab
Use a generated ID such as UNIQUEID() as the key, not a name or phone number
Ref columns create one-to-many links and related lists
Calculate totals in virtual columns, but copy prices that must not change with history

activity.title: Draw a data model
steps: Choose a small business process (orders, bookings, field visits or contributions).
List every kind of thing involved and make each one a table.
Give each table a key column and three to six other columns with their types.
Draw lines for every Ref column and label each one-to-many link.
Write one calculated column and its formula in plain words.
activity.evidence: A photo of your hand-drawn data model with keys, types and references labelled

lessons.title: Platform costs, real opportunities and choosing your niche
objectives: Calculate a client's monthly and yearly platform cost from per-user pricing
Explain the AppSheet free prototyping allowance and when a paid plan is needed
Rank app ideas by business value and build effort
Choose a niche of business type and app type to focus on

blocks.text: Clients rarely ask for 'an app'. They ask to stop losing stock, to know which rider delivered what, or to stop chasing members for records. Your opportunity is in those operational headaches inside businesses and organisations that are too small or too specific for packaged software, and too busy to build anything themselves.

blocks.name: connected-world
blocks.alt: People connected across a world map
blocks.caption: Internal tools are cloud-based, so you can build for clients in your town or abroad.

blocks.text: Understand the platform bill first

Your build fee is paid once. The platform fee is paid every month, usually by the client directly. On AppSheet, building and testing is free: you can use basic app and automation features while prototyping and invite up to **10 test users** at no cost. To deploy to the whole team, the client takes a paid plan. At the time of writing, AppSheet listed **Starter**, **Core** and **Enterprise Plus** plans charged per user per month, at about US$5, US$10 and US$20 respectively, plus a per-app **Publisher Pro** option for public apps without sign-in. Prices change, so always check the official pricing page on the day you quote.

blocks.title: Features decide the plan
blocks.text: Some features need a higher plan. For example, AppSheet security filters, which limit each user to their own rows, need Core or above. List the features a client needs before you choose the plan.

blocks.title: Worked example: the tailoring app's running cost
blocks.context: For example, Nneka's tailoring app from the first lesson will have 4 users after testing. Figures use an illustrative exchange rate of ₦1,600 to US$1; use the real rate on the day.
steps: Starter at about US$5 per user: 4 × 5 = US$20 a month, about 20 × 1,600 = ₦32,000.
Core at about US$10 per user: 4 × 10 = US$40 a month, about 40 × 1,600 = ₦64,000.
Yearly Core cost: 40 × 12 = US$480.
Nneka wants each apprentice to see only their own assigned orders, which needs security filters, so Core is the realistic plan.
blocks.result: Nneka should budget about US$40 a month (roughly ₦64,000 at the illustrative rate) after the free testing stage, and she should hear this before she agrees to any build fee.

blocks.text: Where the work is

items: **Cooperatives and thrift groups:** member contributions, loans and repayments that a secretary now keeps in notebooks.
**Agro-input shops and aggregators:** stock, sales and farmer records across a shop and the field.
**Service businesses:** laundries, tailoring, repairs, cleaning companies tracking jobs and staff.
**NGOs and community programmes:** field visit and beneficiary data collected offline, then synced.
**Logistics and dispatch riders:** pickups, deliveries, cash collected and proof photos.
**Remote clients abroad:** small companies that need an internal tool built on a platform they already pay for.

blocks.text: Ranking ideas: value against effort

blocks.title: Which app ideas to build first
items: Quick wins: build first
Big projects: plan carefully
Small fixes: maybe a spreadsheet
Avoid for now
blocks.caption: High value with low effort, such as a stock and sales tracker, is where a new builder earns trust.

blocks.text: Value means money saved or protected, hours freed, or mistakes prevented. Effort means number of tables, users, rules and integrations. A stock tracker with three tables and five users is a quick win. A customer-facing booking app with online payments is a big project that needs careful scoping.
Foreign-currency fees: check before you promise

Most no-code platforms bill in US dollars by card. For a Nigerian client this brings two practical questions. First, can their card pay a recurring foreign subscription? Some naira cards have international spending limits or block recurring charges, so ask the client to test a payment early. Second, the naira cost moves with the exchange rate, so a fee that is affordable this year can feel heavy next year. Quote the dollar figure, show the naira estimate with the date of the rate you used, and remind the client that the vendor, not you, sets the price.
Choose a niche

A **niche** is the type of client plus the type of app you specialise in, for example 'stock and sales apps for agro-input shops' or 'contribution trackers for cooperatives'. Specialising means your second build reuses the data model of your first, your demos speak the client's language, and referrals come from people in the same trade.

head: Niche question
Why it matters
rows: Do I understand how this trade works day to day?
You will ask better discovery questions and spot missing steps
Can these clients afford the monthly platform fee?
A great app the client cannot keep paying for will be abandoned
Do they already use Google accounts or spreadsheets?
AppSheet starts faster where Google Sheets is familiar
Can I reach ten of them in a month?
Associations, markets and WhatsApp groups make outreach realistic

blocks.title: Health and money data raise the stakes
blocks.text: Clinics, lenders and savings groups hold sensitive personal data. Under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 you must collect only what is needed and keep it secure. Until you are experienced, start with stock, jobs and logistics apps.

takeaways: Platform fees are monthly and per user; the client must budget for them
AppSheet is free for prototyping with up to 10 test users; deployment needs a paid plan
Rank ideas by value and effort and start with quick wins
A clear niche (client type plus app type) makes each build faster and more convincing

activity.title: Cost and rank three app ideas
steps: Write three app ideas for businesses you can reach.
For each, count the users and estimate the monthly platform cost on Starter and Core using today's published prices.
Place each idea on the value and effort matrix.
Choose one niche and write it as one sentence: 'I build ___ apps for ___'.
activity.evidence: A table of three ideas with users, monthly cost and matrix position, plus your one-sentence niche

quiz.q: Tunde keeps a personal list of his 30 clients and is the only person who edits it. What is the best tool?
options: A no-code app with three tables
quiz.explain: One person with a simple list does not need an app. Use the simplest tool that works.

quiz.q: Why is a customer's name a poor key for a Customers table?
options: Two customers can share a name and names can change
quiz.explain: A key must be unique and stable. A generated ID such as UNIQUEID() is the safe choice.

quiz.q: In Bisi's laundry app an order has 3 shirts at ₦800 and 2 trousers at ₦1,000. What is the order total?
A client with 6 staff needs security filters on AppSheet. If Core is about US$10 per user per month, what is the monthly cost?
quiz.explain: Security filters need Core or above: 6 × 10 = US$60 a month.

quiz.q: Where should an order's line total live in a good data model?
options: Typed in by the rider each time
In a calculated virtual column from Qty and price
In a column for each item type
quiz.explain: Values that can be worked out should be calculated, so they never disagree with the data.

modules.title: Building in AppSheet: Data, Logic, Testing and Handover
modules.overview: In this module you build one complete app from start to finish: a stock and sales app for an agro-input shop. You prepare the Google Sheet, generate the app, add calculations, rules and an automatic low-stock alert, then test it, secure it and document it so someone else can run it.

lessons.title: From Google Sheet to working app: setup, column types and views
objectives: Prepare Google Sheets tabs that AppSheet can read cleanly
Generate an AppSheet app and check every column's type, key and label
Create references between tables
Design the main views a shop owner and staff will use

blocks.text: In this module you will build one real app: a **stock and sales app** for an agro-input shop. It tracks products, deliveries into the shop and sales to farmers, and warns the owner when stock runs low. Every step works on the free prototyping stage of AppSheet, so you can follow along with a Google account and a phone or laptop.

blocks.name: customize-app
blocks.alt: A person arranging the screens of a phone app
blocks.caption: In AppSheet you shape the app from your sheet: tables first, then views.

blocks.text: Step 1: prepare the sheet properly
AppSheet reads each tab of a Google Sheet as a table. Most early problems come from messy sheets, so prepare them carefully before you connect anything.

items: One table per tab, with tab names such as Products, Stock In and Sales.
Exactly one header row in row 1, with short, clear column names and no blank headers.
No merged cells, no totals rows, no notes typed under the data and no blank rows in the middle.
An ID column first in every tab. Leave it blank for now; the app will fill it.
Three to five realistic sample rows, so AppSheet can guess column types correctly.

blocks.title: Worked example: Esther's agro-input shop sheet
blocks.context: For example, Esther runs an agro-input shop in Makurdi selling fertiliser, seed and crop protection products. Two sales staff serve farmers. She wants to stop counting bags every evening to know what is left. Prices are illustrative.
steps: Products tab: ProductID, Name, Unit, Price, Opening Stock, Reorder Level. Sample row: NPK 15:15:15, 50kg bag, ₦38,000, 40, 15.
Stock In tab: InID, Date, Product, Qty, Supplier. Sample row: a delivery of 25 bags of NPK.
Sales tab: SaleID, Date, Product, Qty, Unit Price, Customer Phone, Sold By.
She removes a 'TOTAL' row she had typed at the bottom of the Sales tab, because AppSheet would read it as a sale.
She creates the app from the sheet in AppSheet and adds the other two tabs as tables.
blocks.result: Three clean tables are connected: Products, Stock In and Sales. The app opens with a basic screen per table, ready to be configured.

blocks.text: Step 2: fix columns in the table editor

AppSheet guesses settings for every column. Never accept the guesses blindly. Open each table's columns and check four things: the **type**, the **key**, the **label** (the column shown when a row is picked from a list, usually the Name) and the **initial value**.

head: Column
Setting to choose
Why
rows: Unique for every row; staff never type it
Dropdowns show 'NPK 15:15:15', not a random ID
Links each delivery and sale to one product
Shows money properly and uses a number keyboard
Records which signed-in staff member made the sale

blocks.text: If you later add or rename a column in the Google Sheet, AppSheet does not see it automatically. Open the table in the editor and use its option to regenerate the structure, then check the column settings again, because regenerating can reset types you had changed. This is one reason to settle the data model on paper before building: every sheet change costs you a round of re-checking.

Name columns the way the shop talks. If Esther's staff say 'qty' and 'bags', use Qty and Unit; if they say 'customer number', do not call it Contact MSISDN. Column names appear on forms, so plain names are free training.
Step 3: design the views

A **view** is a screen. AppSheet offers several view types, including deck, table, gallery, detail, form, calendar, map, chart and dashboard. Choose them for the user, not for you. Esther's staff stand at a counter with a phone in one hand, so they need few taps and large buttons.

blocks.title: Building order for any AppSheet app
items: Clean the sheet
Set keys and types
Add references
Design views
Add rules and automation
blocks.caption: Follow this order; changing the data after views are built causes rework.

items: **Products** as a deck view with name, price and stock, sorted by name.
**New sale** as a form view placed first in the bottom menu, because it is the most frequent task.
**Sales today** as a table view, built on a **slice** (a filtered subset of a table) with the condition [Date] = TODAY().
**Stock In** as a form for recording deliveries, placed in the side menu because it happens once or twice a week.

blocks.title: Test on the phone, not only the editor
blocks.text: The editor shows a preview, but staff will use real phones in sunlight with busy hands. Install the AppSheet app on an Android phone, open your app, and record a sale yourself before showing anyone.

At this point the app records sales and deliveries, but it cannot yet tell Esther how many bags are left. That calculation, the rules that stop bad entries and the automatic low-stock alert come in the next lesson.

takeaways: Clean sheets first: one header row, no merged cells, no totals rows
Check every column's type, key, label and initial value; never accept guesses blindly
Use Ref columns to link sales and deliveries to products
Put the most frequent task first and use slices for filtered screens

activity.title: Build the first version
steps: Create a Google Sheet with Products, Stock In and Sales tabs for a shop you know, with 3 to 5 sample rows each.
Create an AppSheet app from the sheet and add all three tables.
Set keys, labels, Ref columns and initial values as in the table above.
Create a 'New sale' form, a products deck and a 'Sales today' slice and view.
Record two test sales on your phone.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of your column settings for Sales and of the app on your phone showing a recorded sale

lessons.title: Logic in AppSheet: expressions, validation, actions and bots
objectives: Write AppSheet expressions that calculate stock from linked tables
Add Valid If and Required rules that stop bad entries
Create an action that changes data in one tap
Build a bot that emails the owner when stock falls to the reorder level

blocks.text: Logic is what turns a data-entry screen into a useful tool. In AppSheet, logic is written as **expressions**: short formulas, similar to spreadsheet formulas, that use column names in square brackets and functions such as SELECT, SUM, IF and TODAY. You use expressions in four main places: calculated columns, validation rules, actions and bots.

blocks.name: apps-notifications
blocks.caption: A bot turns data changes into alerts, so the owner hears about low stock without opening the app.

blocks.text: Calculating stock from linked rows

Stock is never typed in. It is calculated from the opening stock, plus everything received, minus everything sold. Add a virtual column called **Current Stock** to the Products table with this App formula:
[Opening Stock] + SUM(SELECT(Stock In[Qty], [Product] = [_THISROW].[ProductID])) - SUM(SELECT(Sales[Qty], [Product] = [_THISROW].[ProductID]))

Read it in plain words: SELECT gathers the Qty values from Stock In rows whose Product matches this product; SUM adds them; the same is done for Sales and subtracted. **[_THISROW]** means 'the product row we are calculating for'.

blocks.title: Worked example: NPK stock after a busy week
blocks.context: For example, in Esther's shop the NPK 15:15:15 product starts the month with an opening stock of 40 bags and a reorder level of 15 bags.
steps: One delivery is recorded in Stock In: 25 bags.
Sales rows for NPK during the week add up to 52 bags.
Current Stock = 40 + 25 - 52 = 13 bags.
13 is at or below the reorder level of 15, so the product should trigger a low-stock alert.
The last sale was 3 bags at ₦38,000 (illustrative), so that sale's value is 3 × 38,000 = ₦114,000.
blocks.result: The app shows 13 bags left without anyone counting, and the bot you build below emails Esther that NPK needs reordering.

blocks.text: Rules that stop mistakes

head: Setting
Expression on the Sales table
What it prevents
rows: A sale saved with no product or quantity
Zero or negative quantities, and selling more bags than the shop holds
Staff retyping prices; the price is copied at the time of sale
Asking every small buyer for a phone number; only bulk buyers are asked

blocks.text: **[_THIS]** in a Valid If means 'the value being typed into this column'. **[Product].[Current Stock]** follows the Ref to the product and reads its stock. Add an error message to each Valid If, such as 'Only 13 bags left', so staff know what went wrong.
Making status visible

Numbers alone are easy to miss on a small screen. Add a second virtual column to Products called Stock Status with the formula IF([Current Stock] <= [Reorder Level], "Reorder", "OK"). Then add a **format rule** that shows Reorder in red. Sort the products deck so Reorder items appear first. Esther now sees what to buy at a glance, and the same Stock Status column can drive a 'To reorder' slice for her supplier calls.

When conditions have more than two outcomes, IFS reads more clearly than nested IFs. For example, IFS([Current Stock] <= 0, "Out", [Current Stock] <= [Reorder Level], "Reorder", TRUE, "OK") checks each condition in order and returns the first match.
Actions: one tap instead of many

An **action** is a button that does something to data. Add a Status column (Enum: Pending payment, Paid) to Sales, then create an action of type 'Data: set the values of some columns in this row' that sets Status to Paid. Add the condition [Status] = "Pending payment" so the button only appears when it makes sense. Staff now confirm a transfer with one tap instead of opening and editing the record.
Bots: automation that runs by itself

A **bot** watches for an **event**, then runs a **process** made of steps, such as sending an email or a notification. Events can be data changes (a row added, updated or deleted) or a schedule, such as every morning.

blocks.title: Low-stock bot
items: Event: a sale is added
Condition: stock at reorder level
Task: email the owner
Owner reorders from supplier
blocks.caption: The bot only fires when both the event and the condition are true.

items: In Automation, create a bot and a new event: table Sales, data change type Adds only.
Set the condition: [Product].[Current Stock] <= [Product].[Reorder Level].
Add a step that sends an email to the owner's address, with a subject such as 'Low stock: <<[Product].[Name]>>'.
In the body, include the current stock and reorder level using the same <<...>> template style.
Record test sales until the condition is met and confirm the email arrives.

blocks.title: Keep heavy formulas few
blocks.text: Every SELECT inside a virtual column runs across whole tables, and virtual columns are recalculated when the app syncs. On a table with thousands of rows, many such columns slow the app noticeably. Use them for the few numbers that matter, and archive old sales to a separate sheet each year.

takeaways: Expressions use [Column] names and functions such as SELECT, SUM and IF
Calculate stock from linked rows; never ask staff to type it
Valid If, Required and Show If stop bad data at the moment of entry
Actions save taps; bots send alerts when an event and condition are both true

activity.title: Add the logic
steps: Add the Current Stock virtual column to your Products table and check it against a manual count.
Add Required and Valid If rules to Sales, with clear error messages.
Create a 'Mark as paid' action with a condition so it only shows on unpaid sales.
Build the low-stock bot and trigger it with test sales.
Write down one rule you tried that did not work and how you fixed it.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of the Current Stock formula, one Valid If error message on the phone, and the low-stock email in your inbox

lessons.title: Testing, access control, offline use and the handover pack
objectives: Write and run a test script that includes edge cases
Control who can sign in and what each role can see or change
Configure offline use and explain the risk of long offline periods
Produce a handover pack another person could maintain from

blocks.text: An app that works when you, the builder, use it carefully is not finished. It is finished when a busy staff member, a weak network and a careless entry cannot break it, and when someone other than you can maintain it. This lesson covers the four checks professionals do before deployment: testing, access, offline behaviour and documentation.

blocks.name: fixing-bugs
blocks.alt: A person fixing bugs on a large screen
blocks.caption: Testing means hunting for the entries that break your rules before real users find them.

blocks.text: Write a test script

A **test script** is a numbered list of things to try, each with the expected result. Include normal cases (a correct sale), **edge cases** (values at the limit, such as selling exactly the last bag) and wrong entries (zero, negative, blanks, duplicates). Record pass or fail for each, fix the failures and test again.

blocks.title: Worked example: testing Esther's app
blocks.context: For example, Amina is a no-code builder finishing Esther's stock and sales app. She writes 14 test cases and runs them on an Android phone signed in as a sales staff test user.
steps: 11 of 14 cases pass, so 3 fail.
Fail 1: a quantity of 0 was saved. She had written Valid If [_THIS] <= stock but forgot [_THIS] > 0, so she changes it to the AND() version.
Fail 2: two products named 'Maize seed 10kg' could be created. She adds a Valid If on Name: NOT(IN([_THIS], SELECT(Products[Name], [ProductID] <> [_THISROW].[ProductID]))).
Fail 3: a staff test user could edit the opening stock. She makes Opening Stock editable only for the owner (see roles below).
She reruns all 14 cases, not just the 3 that failed, because fixes can break other things.
blocks.result: All 14 cases pass on the second run. The test log, with dates and results, goes into the handover pack as proof of quality.

blocks.text: Control access

items: **Sign-in:** require users to sign in, and share the app only with the named email addresses of staff.

**Roles:** keep a small Users table (Email, Role). Use expressions such as LOOKUP(USEREMAIL(), "Users", "Email", "Role") = "Owner" in Editable If or Show If to limit who changes prices and opening stock.

**Security filters:** a Yes/No expression per table, such as [Sold By] = USEREMAIL(), that keeps rows a user should not have out of their app. They need the Core plan or above, and Google advises protecting sensitive data at the data source level too.
**The sheet itself:** anyone with edit access to the Google Sheet can change data directly. Share the sheet only with the owner and the builder.

blocks.title: Personal data and the law
blocks.text: Customer phone numbers are personal data. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 expects you to collect only what you need, tell people why, and keep it secure. Do not collect BVN, NIN or card details in a no-code app, and remove test users who have left before go-live.
Offline use

AppSheet stores the app definition and data on the phone, so staff can keep recording when the network drops. The app must first be opened while online. Edits made offline are queued and sent when the connection returns. Settings such as **Delayed sync** (queue changes until the user syncs) and **Sync on start** (force a sync when the app opens) let you balance data cost against freshness.

blocks.title: Long offline periods cause overwrites
blocks.text: Google's documentation warns that if a phone stays offline for days or weeks and then syncs, its older edits can override changes other users made in the meantime. Train field staff to sync at least daily, and design tables so each person mostly adds new rows rather than editing shared ones.

blocks.title: Go-live checklist
items: Test script all passed
Sign-in and roles set
Offline sync tested
Deployment check passed
Handover pack delivered
blocks.caption: Do not move the app to a paid plan and real users until every box is ticked.

blocks.text: Test offline behaviour on purpose: switch a test phone to airplane mode, record two sales, reconnect, sync and confirm both rows reached the Google Sheet with the right staff email and date.
The handover pack

Documentation lets the client, or another builder, keep the app alive. Keep it short and practical. AppSheet's **Deployment check** in the editor flags common problems before you deploy, so run it and note the result.

head: Section
What it contains
rows: A diagram of tables, keys and references, and the location of the Google Sheet
Every virtual column, Valid If, action and bot, in plain words and as written
Who has access, their role, and how to add or remove a user
Sync at least daily; how to record a delivery; what to do if a sale is wrong
Which Google account owns the app, the plan and its monthly cost
The test script with dates and results

takeaways: Test normal cases, edge cases and wrong entries, then rerun everything after fixes
Combine sign-in, roles, security filters and sheet sharing to control access
Offline works well for short gaps; long offline periods can overwrite others' changes
A handover pack makes the app maintainable by someone other than you

activity.title: Test, secure and document
steps: Write a test script of at least 12 cases for your app, including 4 edge or wrong-entry cases.
Run it on a phone as a non-owner test user and record pass or fail.
Fix failures, add a Users table with roles, and rerun all cases.
Switch the phone to airplane mode, record a sale, reconnect and confirm it reaches the sheet.
Write a one-to-two page handover pack using the six sections above.
activity.evidence: Your completed test log and handover pack

quiz.q: Opening stock is 30 bags, deliveries total 20 and sales total 41. The reorder level is 10. What should the app show?
quiz.explain: 30 + 20 - 41 = 9, which is at or below 10, so the bot condition is true.

quiz.q: Which AppSheet setting stops a staff member from saving a sale with a quantity of zero?
quiz.explain: Valid If checks the value as it is typed and blocks the save if the expression is false.

quiz.q: Why should Unit Price on a sale use [Product].[Price] as an initial value rather than a virtual column?
options: Initial values are faster to type
So the price at the time of sale is kept even if the product price changes later
AppSheet does not allow virtual columns on Sales
quiz.explain: An initial value copies the price once. A virtual column would always read today's price and rewrite history.

quiz.q: A field officer has been offline for two weeks. What is the main risk when she syncs?
options: Her phone will lose the app
The app will charge extra data fees
Her older edits may override changes other users made meanwhile
quiz.explain: Google's documentation warns that late syncs can apply old updates over newer changes by others.

quiz.q: After fixing 3 failed test cases, what should the builder do next?
quiz.explain: A fix can break something that passed before, so the whole script is run again.

modules.title: Client Work: Discovery, Pricing and Your Practice
modules.overview: Building is half the job. This module shows you how to run a discovery session that finds the real process and its cost, how to price a build and its ongoing support without underpricing yourself, and how to turn your projects into a portfolio and a 90-day plan for paid no-code work.

lessons.title: Discovery: mapping the client's process and writing the app specification
objectives: Run a structured discovery conversation with a client
Map the current process step by step and measure the time it costs
Turn findings into user stories sorted as Must, Should and Could
Write a one-page app specification the client can approve

blocks.text: **Discovery** is the conversation and observation you do before quoting or building. Its purpose is to understand the real process, the people who do it and what it costs today. Builders who skip discovery build the app the client described, which is often not the app the client needs.

blocks.name: interview
blocks.alt: Two people in a structured conversation
blocks.caption: Good discovery is mostly listening and watching how the work is really done.

blocks.text: Questions that find the real problem

head: Area
Question to ask
What you learn
rows: Walk me through what happens from the moment this starts until it is finished.
The real steps, including the ones nobody wrote down
Where does it go wrong? Tell me about the last time.
Concrete failures you can design against
How long does each step take, and how often?
Hours you can measure and later show were saved
Who enters data, who reads it, and what phones do they use?
Can I see the notebook, sheet or WhatsApp messages you use now?
The real fields and the messy cases
In three months, how will you know the app was worth it?
A measurable goal for the proposal

blocks.text: Ask to **watch** the process happen once, even for 20 minutes. People describe their work as tidier than it is. What they do with a pen and a phone is the truth your app must handle.

blocks.title: From conversation to specification
items: Interview and observe
Map current steps
Measure time and errors
Write user stories
One-page specification
blocks.caption: Each stage feeds the next; the specification is what the client approves.

blocks.title: Worked example: a thrift cooperative in Owerri
blocks.context: For example, Ruth is the secretary of a women's thrift cooperative in Owerri with 48 members. Members contribute weekly. She records each payment in a notebook from WhatsApp transfer screenshots, then reconciles the notebook with the bank statement at month end. Times are her own estimates.
steps: Weekly recording: about 3 minutes per member, so 48 × 3 = 144 minutes, which is 2.4 hours a week.
Monthly: 2.4 hours × 4 weeks = 9.6 hours, plus about 5 hours of month-end reconciliation, giving 14.6 hours a month.
Errors: twice in the last quarter a member was told she had not paid when she had.
Users: Ruth enters payments; the treasurer and chairperson view reports; members do not need to sign in.
Success measure agreed with Ruth: month-end reconciliation finished in under 2 hours, and no disputed payments.
blocks.result: The problem is about 14.6 hours of secretary time a month plus disputes that damage trust. The app is a payments register linked to a members table, with a monthly statement per member, not a members' mobile banking app.

blocks.text: When the client arrives with a solution

Clients often open with a solution: 'I want an app like the bank's' or 'I need a dashboard'. Do not argue and do not agree yet. Ask what that solution would let them do that they cannot do today, and keep asking until you reach a step in the process and a cost. Ruth first asked for 'an app where members log in', but the real pain was her own recording time and payment disputes, which a much smaller internal app solves.

items: **Red flag:** nobody can say who will enter the data every day. Apps without an owner die within weeks.
**Red flag:** the client wants every feature in version one and cannot name the most important one.
**Red flag:** sensitive data with no agreement on who may see it.
**Good sign:** one decision maker, a clear daily user and a measurable pain.

blocks.text: User stories and priorities

A **user story** describes one need in the form: 'As a [role], I want [action] so that [benefit].' For example: 'As the secretary, I want to record a payment by choosing a member and amount so that I stop rewriting names.' Sort stories into **Must** (the app is useless without it), **Should** (important, but can follow) and **Could** (nice to have). This is the MoSCoW method, where the W stands for 'Won't have this time'.

items: Must: record payments against members; show each member's total for the month; flag members who have not paid by Friday.
Should: a monthly statement each member can be sent as a PDF.
Could: a chart of total contributions per month for the annual meeting.
Won't (this time): members logging in to see their own balance.

blocks.text: The one-page specification

Your specification fits on one page: the problem in two sentences, the users and roles, the data model sketch, the Must and Should stories, the platform and its monthly cost, what is out of scope, and the success measure. The client signs or approves it in writing, even by WhatsApp message, before you quote a final price.

blocks.title: Money data needs extra care
blocks.text: A contributions app holds personal and financial records. Agree who may see what, keep the sheet shared only with officers, and never store members' bank login details, BVN or card numbers.

takeaways: Discovery finds the real process, the people and the cost before you quote
Watch the work happen; descriptions are tidier than reality
Measure hours and errors now so you can show the improvement later
User stories sorted with MoSCoW keep the first version small and useful

activity.title: Run a mini discovery
steps: Interview a real business owner or group officer for 30 minutes using the six questions.
Map their current process as numbered steps and note time per step.
Calculate the monthly hours the process takes, showing your arithmetic.
Write at least six user stories and sort them with MoSCoW.
Draft the one-page specification.
activity.evidence: Your process map, time calculation and one-page specification

lessons.title: Pricing a no-code build, writing the proposal and controlling scope
objectives: Estimate a build in hours by phase and add a contingency
Separate the build fee, the platform subscription and ongoing support
Write a proposal with deliverables, exclusions and payment milestones
Handle change requests without losing money or goodwill

blocks.text: Underpricing is the most common mistake new builders make, because the visible part of the work, clicking in the editor, is quick. Most time goes into discovery, testing, training and fixing the things users discover. Price the whole job, and keep three costs clearly separate: your **build fee**, the client's **platform subscription** and **ongoing support**.

blocks.name: contract-signed
blocks.caption: A clear written proposal protects both you and the client when requests change.

blocks.text: Estimate by phase

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing the cooperative payments app
blocks.context: For example, Ruth's cooperative from the last lesson approves the specification. The builder's rate is ₦10,000 per hour, an illustrative figure; set your own from your skill and market.
steps: Hours by phase: discovery and specification 6, data model and sheet setup 4, building views, rules and statement 16, testing 6, training and handover 4.
Total: 6 + 4 + 16 + 6 + 4 = 36 hours.
Contingency of 15% for unknowns: 360,000 × 1.15 = ₦414,000.
Milestones of 40%, 40% and 20%: ₦165,600 on approval, ₦165,600 when the test version is shown, ₦82,800 at go-live.
blocks.result: The proposal quotes ₦414,000 for the build in three payments that add back to ₦414,000, separate from the platform fee the cooperative pays directly.

blocks.text: The platform fee belongs to the client

Set up the app under an account the client owns, or plan a clear transfer, and have the client pay the platform directly. If you pay and recharge it, the app stops the day your card fails or the relationship ends. For the cooperative, three officers would use the app; at about US$5 per user on Starter that is around US$15 a month at the time of writing. State the plan, user count and that prices are set by the vendor.
Check the value before you send the quote

A client pays happily when the app clearly earns more than it costs. Do a simple **payback** check: take the monthly benefit (money saved or protected, plus staff time freed, valued honestly), subtract the monthly platform fee, and divide the build fee by what is left. The answer is the number of months before the app has paid for itself.

For example, with illustrative figures: a provision shop believes it loses about ₦50,000 a month through unrecorded sales. The platform fee is about ₦24,000 a month (US$15 at the illustrative rate of ₦1,600). The net monthly benefit is 50,000 - 24,000 = ₦26,000. A build fee of ₦300,000 pays back in 300,000 ÷ 26,000, about 11.5 months. If payback runs well beyond a year, offer a smaller first phase with only the Must stories, or fewer paid users, rather than cutting your hourly rate.
Support after go-live

Offer either a **retainer** (a fixed monthly fee for a set number of hours, such as 4 hours a month at your rate, which would be ₦40,000 at ₦10,000 per hour) or **pay-as-you-go** support at an hourly rate. Include a short free warranty period, such as 14 days, for fixing defects in what was agreed. A defect is something that does not work as specified; a new idea is a change.

blocks.title: Project and payment timeline
items: Spec approved: 40% paid
Build and test
Test version shown: 40% paid
Training and go-live: 20% paid
Warranty, then support
blocks.caption: Tie each payment to something the client can see.

blocks.text: What the proposal must contain

head: Section
Example wording
rows: A payments register app on AppSheet with members, payments and monthly statements, for 3 officer users
Member log-in, bank integration, SMS sending and data entry of past years' records
Provide the member list within 3 days; pay the platform subscription; name one decision maker
Test version in 2 weeks after the first payment; go-live 1 week after acceptance
₦414,000 in three milestones; support at ₦10,000 per hour or a ₦40,000 monthly retainer
New requests are estimated in hours and approved in writing before work starts

blocks.text: Controlling scope

**Scope creep** is the slow growth of the job through small extra requests. Each one sounds tiny; together they eat your profit. Answer every request the same calm way: thank the client, check it against the specification, and if it is new, give an hour estimate and ask whether to add it now or put it in the next phase. Keep a simple change log with the date, request, hours and approval, so the final invoice has no surprises.

blocks.title: Payment scams target freelancers too
blocks.text: Never start work on a fake 'transfer alert' screenshot. Confirm the money in your own bank or Paystack, Opay or Moniepoint account before each milestone. Be wary of overpayments followed by requests to refund the difference.

takeaways: Estimate every phase, not just building, and add a contingency
Keep build fee, platform subscription and support clearly separate
Tie payments to milestones the client can see
Handle extra requests with an hour estimate and written approval

activity.title: Price and propose
steps: Estimate hours by phase for the app you specified in the last lesson.
Choose your hourly rate and calculate the fee with a contingency, checking your sums.
Split the fee into three milestones that add back to the total.
Write a one-to-two page proposal with all six sections.
Write the reply you would send to a client asking for 'just one more report' after approval.
activity.evidence: Your proposal with the hour estimate, milestone table and the change-request reply

lessons.title: Case studies, demo apps and a 90-day plan for paid no-code work
objectives: Write a short case study that shows problem, build and measured result
Prepare a safe demo app with sample data
Plan outreach in your chosen niche with weekly targets
Set a 90-day plan that moves from demo apps to paid work

blocks.text: Clients buy no-code work when they can see a working app that solves a problem like theirs. Your portfolio is therefore not a list of platforms you know. It is two or three **demo apps** they can tap through, and short **case studies** that explain the thinking and the result.

blocks.name: portfolio-website
blocks.alt: A portfolio website showing project cards
blocks.caption: A small portfolio of real, tappable apps beats a long list of tools.

blocks.text: Build safe demo apps

items: Copy your project into a demo version filled with **made-up sample data**: invented names, numbers like 0800 000 0001 and test emails. Never show a real client's customers.
Ask permission before naming any client, and describe them generally (for example, 'a thrift cooperative in the South East') if they prefer.
Keep the demo on the free prototyping stage and share it with prospects as test users, staying within the 10-user limit.
Record your own short screen recording of the app on a phone and keep it on your portfolio page or WhatsApp catalogue.

blocks.text: Write case studies that persuade

A good case study is 150 to 300 words with five parts: the **client and problem**, the **old process and its cost**, **what you built** (tables, key rules, automation), the **measured result**, and a **lesson learned**. Real numbers, even small ones, convince more than adjectives. If you do not have a measurement yet, say so honestly and show the before figures.

head: Part
Example from the cooperative app
rows: A secretary spent about 14.6 hours a month recording and reconciling 48 members' contributions
Members and Payments tables, an unpaid-by-Friday list, a monthly statement per member
Reported by the client after two months; quote her figures only with permission
Watching one Friday's recording session revealed that screenshots arrive in batches, so a quick-add form mattered most

blocks.text: Where to show your work

Keep it simple and cheap on data. A single portfolio page or a free website section with your case studies, your WhatsApp Business catalogue with one item per demo app, and a LinkedIn profile that names your niche are enough to start. Each case study should end with one clear next step, such as 'Message me for a 20-minute walkthrough of the demo'.
Outreach that respects people's time

A good first message is short and specific. Name the trade, name the problem you solve, offer something small and concrete, and make it easy to say no. For example: 'Good afternoon, Madam. I build simple phone apps for agro-input shops that show stock left without counting bags each evening. Could I show you a 10-minute demo on my phone when you are less busy this week?' Visit in person where you can; a demo on your phone at the shop counter is more convincing than any link.
Your 90-day plan

blocks.title: 90 days to paid work
items: Weeks 1-4: two demo apps
Weeks 5-8: outreach and discovery
Weeks 9-12: first paid builds
blocks.caption: Each phase produces evidence that makes the next phase easier.

blocks.title: Worked example: Aisha's 90-day plan
blocks.context: For example, Aisha, a former shop manager in Kano, chooses the niche 'stock and sales apps for agro-input and provision shops'. She has about 10 hours a week. Her targets are illustrative goals, not promised results.
steps: Weeks 1 to 4: build two demo apps (agro-input stock and provision shop sales), about 15 hours each, which is 30 of her 40 available hours; the rest goes on case-study write-ups.
Weeks 5 to 8: list 40 shops through her market association and WhatsApp groups and contact 10 a week, so 4 × 10 = 40 contacts.
From those 40, she aims for 6 discovery conversations and 3 proposals.
Weeks 9 to 12: aim to win 1 or 2 builds, deliver the first using the full test and handover process, and ask for a testimonial at go-live.
Every Friday she records contacts made, conversations held, proposals sent and money received in a simple sheet.
blocks.result: By day 90 Aisha has two demos, two case studies, a tracked pipeline of 40 contacts and, if her targets hold, her first paid build. Her weekly sheet shows where to adjust.

blocks.text: Keep growing your skill

items: Work through Google's official AppSheet help centre topics on expressions, automation and security after each project.
Rebuild one demo on a second platform, such as Glide, to learn which client needs suit which tool.
Learn basic SQL and data modelling; they deepen everything you do in no-code.
Lead others: run a short demo session for your cooperative, association or WODDI circle and teach the five-question test from this course.

blocks.title: Charge for your second build
blocks.text: One free or discounted build for a case study is reasonable. After that, quote properly. Your demos and process are your proof.

takeaways: Clients buy what they can tap through: keep two or three safe demo apps
Use invented sample data and get permission before naming clients
Case studies need the old cost, what you built and an honest result
Track weekly activity so your 90-day plan can be adjusted

activity.title: Build your practice plan
steps: Create a demo copy of your app with invented sample data.
Write a 150 to 300 word case study using the five parts.
Write your 90-day plan with weekly targets for building, contacts, conversations and proposals.
Set up a tracking sheet with one row per week and columns for each target.
activity.evidence: Your demo app link, case study and 90-day tracking sheet

quiz.q: During discovery, a client says their process is 'simple'. What should you do next?
options: Ask to watch the process happen once
quiz.explain: Observing the real work reveals steps and messy cases that descriptions leave out.

quiz.q: A secretary spends 2 minutes per member weekly for 60 members, plus 4 hours of month-end work. About how many hours a month is that, using 4 weeks?
quiz.explain: 60 × 2 = 120 minutes = 2 hours a week; 2 × 4 = 8 hours; 8 + 4 = 12 hours.

quiz.q: A build is estimated at 30 hours at ₦8,000 per hour with a 10% contingency. What is the fee?
Who should normally pay the monthly platform subscription?
options: The client, directly, under an account they own or control
The builder, without telling the client
Nobody, because the free plan is enough for deployment
quiz.explain: If the client owns and pays for the platform, the app keeps running whatever happens to the builder.

quiz.q: After approval, a client asks for an SMS feature that was listed under exclusions. What is the best reply?
options: Add it free to keep them happy
Remove another feature without telling them
Estimate it in hours and ask whether to add it now or later, in writing
quiz.explain: Change requests are estimated and approved in writing, which protects both sides.

finalQuiz.q: Which situation most clearly calls for a no-code app rather than a spreadsheet?
options: Four staff on phones recording linked orders where mistakes cost money
finalQuiz.explain: Several users, phones, linked records and costly mistakes are the signs an app earns its place.

finalQuiz.q: What is the safest key for a Customers table in AppSheet?
options: A generated ID such as UNIQUEID()
finalQuiz.explain: A generated ID is unique and never changes, unlike names or phone numbers.

finalQuiz.q: In a laundry app, why are clothes stored in an Order Items table instead of columns Item1, Item2, Item3?
options: So an order can have any number of items without changing the structure
Because AppSheet forbids more than three columns
To make the sheet look longer
finalQuiz.explain: One row per item handles any order size; fixed item columns break when a customer brings more.

finalQuiz.q: A client with 8 users needs security filters. At about US$10 per user per month on Core, what is the yearly platform cost?
finalQuiz.explain: 8 × 10 = US$80 a month; 80 × 12 = US$960 a year.

finalQuiz.q: What does [_THISROW] mean inside the Current Stock formula on the Products table?
options: The product row the formula is calculating for
The last row added to Sales
The first row of the sheet
finalQuiz.explain: [_THISROW] refers to the current row, so SELECT matches sales and deliveries for this product.

finalQuiz.q: Opening stock 50, received 30, sold 68, reorder level 10. What happens?
finalQuiz.explain: 50 + 30 - 68 = 12, which is above 10, so the condition [Current Stock] <= [Reorder Level] is false.

finalQuiz.q: Which AppSheet feature sends the owner an email automatically when a sale meets a condition?
options: A bot with an event, condition and email step
finalQuiz.explain: Bots watch for events, check a condition and run tasks such as sending email.

finalQuiz.q: A staff test user could edit the opening stock. What is the best fix?
options: Ask staff not to touch it
Make it editable only for the Owner role using a Users table and Editable If
finalQuiz.explain: Role checks with LOOKUP(USEREMAIL(), ...) limit who can change sensitive fields.

finalQuiz.q: Which is the clearest example of an edge case to include in a test script?
options: Selling exactly the last bag in stock
finalQuiz.explain: Edge cases sit at the limits of your rules, where errors most often hide.

finalQuiz.q: In MoSCoW prioritisation, 'members logging in to see their balance' was put under W. What does that mean?
options: It won't be built in this version
finalQuiz.explain: W means 'Won't have this time': agreed as out of scope for now.

finalQuiz.q: A build of 40 hours at ₦9,000 per hour has a 15% contingency and milestones of 40/40/20. What is the final 20% payment?
What should a demo app in your portfolio contain?
options: Invented sample data, shared with prospects as test users
finalQuiz.explain: Demo apps use made-up data to protect privacy and let prospects tap through a working app.

capstone.title: No-Code App Build Project
capstone.brief: Plan, build and price a complete internal app on Google AppSheet for a real or realistic business: a planning document (target users, data model and core workflows), a tested working app with a handover pack, and a pricing proposal with a 90-day plan for no-code client work.
steps: Choose a real business or group and run a discovery session using the six question areas; measure the current process in hours and errors.
Write the planning document: problem, target users and roles, data model diagram with keys and references, user stories sorted with MoSCoW, and the success measure.
Prepare the Google Sheet and build the app in AppSheet with at least three linked tables, a calculated virtual column, Valid If rules, one action and one bot.
Write and run a test script of at least 12 cases on a phone as a non-owner user, fix failures and rerun all cases; test offline recording and sync.
Write the handover pack: data model, rules, users and roles, daily routine, accounts and costs, and the test log.
Write a proposal pricing the build by phase with contingency and milestones, separating the platform fee and support, then add your 90-day plan with weekly targets.
evidence: Planning document with data model diagram and prioritised user stories
Link to the working app shared as a test user, with screenshots of key screens
Completed test log showing all cases passed after fixes
Handover pack of one to two pages
Pricing proposal with hour estimate, milestones and exclusions
